summary: Describes how Open Pluggable Edge Services addresses the nine architecture-level considerations raised by the Internet Architecture Board. It shows how the framework responds to the IAB's concerns.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3914 is the OPES working group's answer to the Internet Architecture Board's criticisms. For each of the nine concerns it shows which part of the OPES design deals with it, and it is frank about the cases where the answer is incomplete, such as when a device only reads the traffic without changing it.

questions: how does opes address iab concerns
subtitle: How the OPES framework answers the nine architectural worries the Internet Architecture Board raised

tldr.problem: The Internet Architecture Board set out nine architectural concerns about OPES, a framework that lets a network device rewrite the application messages passing through it, and the working group had to show that each one was dealt with.
tldr.mechanism: The memo goes through the nine considerations one at a time and points to the OPES mechanism that answers each: consent requirements, IP-level addressability, traces carried in the application protocol, a bypass feature, and identification that lets a user look up an intermediary's privacy policy.
tldr.outcome: Several answers are honest about their limits. Tracing only helps where the application protocol supports it, a processor that merely reads content without changing it cannot be detected at all, and a notification protocol was deliberately not built because it would have doubled the sender's message count.

facts.label: Trace direction
facts.value: Follows the application message to its recipient

facts.label: Notification direction
facts.value: Back to the sender, the opposite way to a trace

today: RFC 3914 is an Informational memo from October 2004 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines no mechanisms of its own, and its security considerations section says only that the security of the OPES mechanisms is discussed in the corresponding sections of the other OPES framework documents.

sections.title: Nine Questions from the IAB
sections.content:
The Open Pluggable Edge Services architecture enables cooperative application services between a data provider, a data consumer and zero or more OPES processors, and the services under consideration analyse and possibly transform application-level messages exchanged between the provider and the consumer.

In the process of chartering OPES, the IAB made recommendations on issues that OPES solutions should be required to address, formulated in the form of a specific IAB considerations document. The IAB emphasised that its considerations did not recommend specific solutions and did not mandate specific functional requirements. Addressing a consideration may involve showing appropriate protocol mechanisms or demonstrating that the issue does not apply, and addressing a consideration does not necessarily mean supporting the technology implied by the wording.

The primary goal of this document is to show that all formal IAB recommendations are addressed by OPES, to the extent that those considerations can be addressed by an IETF working group, and the limitations of the OPES working group to address certain aspects are explicitly documented. The IAB considerations document contains many informal recommendations as well; for example, while the IAB informally requires the OPES architecture to protect end-to-end data integrity by supporting end-host detection of and response to inappropriate behaviour by OPES intermediaries, the IAB chose to formalize these requirements through a set of more specific recommendations, such as the notification considerations. The OPES framework addresses informal IAB recommendations by addressing the corresponding formal considerations. There are nine formal IAB considerations that OPES has to address, and in the core of the document are the corresponding nine consideration sections, each containing general discussion as well as references to the specific OPES mechanisms relevant to it.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB did not say how to build OPES. It said there were nine things a good design would have to deal with, and this memo is the working group's account of how its design deals with each one.

sections.title: One-Party Consent
sections.content:
The IAB consideration is that an OPES framework standardized in the IETF must require that the use of any OPES service be explicitly authorized by one of the application-layer end-hosts, that is, either the content provider or the client.

The OPES architecture requires that OPES processors must be consented to by either the data consumer or data provider application. While this requirement directly satisfies the IAB concern, no requirement alone can prevent consent-less introduction of OPES processors: the framework requires one-party consent but cannot guarantee it in the presence of incompliant OPES entities.

The OPES architecture enables concerned parties to detect unwanted OPES processors by examining OPES traces, and while the use of traces is mandatory, a tracing mechanism on its own cannot detect processors that are in violation of the OPES specifications, for example processors operating in stealth mode. The architecture does, however, allow the use of a content signature to verify the authenticity of performed adaptations. Content signatures are a strong but expensive mechanism that can detect any modification of signed content, provided that the content provider is willing to sign the data and the client is willing either to check the signature or to relay the received content to the provider for verification.

OPES entities may copy or otherwise access content without modifying it, and such access cannot be detected using content signatures. Passive OPES entities can therefore operate on signed content without the consent of the consumer or provider. If content privacy is a concern, content encryption can be used. A passive processor is no different from any intermediary operating outside the OPES framework, and no OPES mechanism, existing or foreseeable, can prevent non-modifying access to content.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is that either the sender or the receiver has to agree before a device may change the traffic. That rule cannot be enforced against a device that ignores it, so the framework also gives people a way to spot changes: signatures on the content and traces left in the message.

sections.title: IP-Layer Communications
sections.content:
The IAB consideration is that for an OPES framework standardized in the IETF, the OPES intermediary must be explicitly addressed at the IP layer by the end user. The OPES architecture requires that OPES processors must be addressable at the IP layer by the end user, the data consumer application.

Both the IAB and the architecture documents mention an important exception: addressing the first OPES processor in a chain of processors is sufficient, because a chain of processors is viewed as a single OPES system at the address of the first chain element. The notion of a chain is not strictly defined by the IAB, so for this purpose a group of OPES processors working on a given application transaction is considered. Such a group would necessarily form a single processing chain with a single exit processor, the one that adapted the given message last, and the architecture essentially requires that last processor to be explicitly addressable at the IP layer by the data consumer application. The chain formation, including its exit point, may depend on an application message and other dynamic factors such as the time of day or system load.

If OPES processing is an internal step at the data consumer or data provider side, the last processor may reside in a private address space and may not be explicitly addressable from outside. In such situations the processing side must designate an addressable point on the same processing chain. That designated point may not, strictly speaking, be an OPES processor, but it will serve as such as far as the IAB considerations are concerned: the data consumer application will be able to address it explicitly at the IP layer and it will represent the processing chain to the outside world.

Designating an addressable processing point avoids the conflict between a narrow reading of the IAB consideration and real system designs. It is irrational to expect a content provider to provide access to internal hosts taking part in content generation, whether OPES processors are involved or not, and internal processors are not likely to be able to answer a consumer's queries, being completely out of the content generation context. For example, an OPES processor adding customer-specific information to XML pages may not understand the final HTML content the consumer receives and may not be able to map the end user request to any internal user identification. Since OPES requires the end of the message processing chain to be addressable, the conflict does not exist: OPES places no requirements on the internal architecture of data producer systems, while requiring the entire content production system to be addressable at the IP layer.
sections.plainLanguage: You should be able to point at the device that is changing your traffic, by its IP address. If the real work happens inside a provider's private network, that provider has to nominate one point that stands for the whole chain.

sections.title: Notification and Tracing
sections.content:
OPES concentrates on tracing rather than notification. The OPES Communications specification defines an OPES trace as application message information about OPES entities that adapted the message, so the trace follows the application message it traces and is for the recipient of that message. Traces are implemented as extensions of the application protocols being adapted and traced. Provider notification, as implied by the IAB, notifies the sender of the application message rather than the recipient, so notifications propagate in the opposite direction of traces. Supporting notifications directly would require a new protocol.

Because notifications cannot be piggy-backed on application messages, they create new messages and may double the number of messages the sender has to process, and the number grows if several intermediaries on the path generate them. Associating notifications with application messages may require duplicating application message information and maintaining sender state until the notification arrives, which increases the overhead. The level of detail in notifications is another concern: experience shows that content providers often require very detailed information about user actions to be interested in notifications at all. The Hit Metering protocol was designed to supply content providers with proxy cache hit counts, in an effort to reduce cache busting behaviour caused by providers' desire for accurate access counts, but it is not widely deployed because it does not supply information such as client IP addresses, browser versions or cookies.

Hit Metering is relevant because it was designed to do for HTTP caching intermediaries what OPES notifications are meant to do for OPES intermediaries. Performance requirements call for state reduction through aggregation of notifications, while provider preferences call for state preservation or duplication, and balancing the two when the sides belong to different organisations with different priorities may be impossible. So instead of explicitly supporting notifications at the protocol level, OPES concentrates on tracing facilities: in essence, OPES supports notifications indirectly, using tracing. The IAB choice of the Notification label is interpreted as Notification assistance, making notifications meaningful, and not as a Notification protocol. The above concerns call for making notification optional.

The architecture does allow an efficient and meaningful notification protocol in certain environments. For example, an OPES callout server attached to a gateway or firewall may scan outgoing traffic for signs of worm or virus activity and notify a local intrusion detection system of potentially compromised hosts inside the network, using OPES tracing information to pinpoint the infected host, which could itself be another OPES entity. In such an example the notifications are sent back to the content producer, the local network, and use OPES tracing to supply details. Content Delivery Networks are another environment where notification using OPES tracing is possible: a CDN node may use several content adaptation services to customise generic content, for example a callout service that inserts advertisements for client-local events. The node itself may not understand the specifics of the ad insertion algorithm implemented at the callout servers, but it may use information in the OPES trace to notify the content producer, for example about the number of advertisements inserted or the number of ad clicks the customer made.

For the IAB's first notification consideration, that the framework needs to assist content providers in detecting and responding to client-centric actions by OPES intermediaries deemed inappropriate, tracing helps because a compliant intermediary or system notifies the content provider of its presence by including its tracing information in the application protocol requests. An OPES system must leave its trace. Detection assistance has its limits: some intermediaries may work exclusively on responses and may not have a chance to trace the request, and some application protocols may not have explicit requests, such as a content push service. Traces must include identification of OPES systems and should include a list of the adaptation actions performed on the provider's content, and this information may be included in the application request, although usually it is included in the application response, an adapted version of which does not reach the content provider. If OPES endpoints cooperate, notification can be assisted with traces. Content providers that suspect or experience difficulties can check whether the requests they receive pass through OPES intermediaries, which is only possible for request and response protocols, request OPES traces from potentially affected users, query for more information where a trace indicates that more is available, or, if everything else fails, enforce a no-adaptation policy using the appropriate OPES bypass mechanisms and end-to-end encryption. Detection and response assistance is limited to application protocols with support for tracing extensions: HTTP has such support, while DNS over UDP does not.

For the second notification consideration, that the framework should assist end users in detecting the behaviour of OPES intermediaries, potentially allowing them to identify imperfect or compromised intermediaries, the same tracing mechanism helps, since a compliant intermediary notifies the end user of its presence by including its tracing information in the application protocol messages sent to the client. Here too an OPES system must leave its trace, and here too there are limits: some systems may work exclusively on requests and never trace the response, and some application protocols have no explicit responses, such as an event logging service. Again, assistance is limited to application protocols with tracing extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: OPES leaves a note in the message saying who changed it and what they did, so the person receiving it can see. The IAB asked for the opposite, a note sent back to the sender, and the memo explains why that was not built: it would have doubled the messages the sender had to handle.

sections.title: Non-blocking, URI Resolution and Reference Validity
sections.content:
The IAB's non-blocking consideration is that if a non-OPES version of content is available from the content provider, the OPES architecture must not prevent users from retrieving it. OPES entities must support a bypass feature: if an application message includes bypass instructions and an OPES intermediary is not configured to ignore them, the matching intermediary will not process the message. An intermediary may be configured to ignore bypass instructions only if no non-OPES version of the content is available. Bypass may generate content errors, since some OPES services may be essential but may not be configured as such, and bypass support has limitations similar to the two notification related considerations.

On URI resolution, the IAB requires that OPES documentation be clear in describing these services as being applied to the result of URI resolution, not as URI resolution itself. The OPES use cases specification documents content adaptations that are in scope, including adaptation of requests and responses, and these do not include URI resolution. In some environments it is technically possible to use documented OPES mechanisms to resolve URIs and other identifiers. For example, a CDN node may substitute domain names in URLs with CDN-chosen IP addresses, essentially performing a URI resolution on behalf of the content producer, and an OPES callout service running on a user PC may rewrite all HTML-embedded advertisement URLs to point to a user-specified local image, essentially performing a URI redirection on behalf of the content consumer. Such URI manipulations are outside the OPES framework scope but cannot be effectively eliminated from the real world.

On reference validity, the IAB requires that all proposed services define their impact on inter- and intra-document reference validity. The OPES framework does not propose adaptation services, but its tracing requirements include identification of OPES intermediaries and services, and it is required that the identification provided can be used to locate information about those intermediaries, including the description of the impact on reference validity.

On addressing extensions, the IAB requires that any services that cannot be achieved while respecting the other two considerations may be reviewed as potential requirements for Internet application addressing architecture extensions, but must not be undertaken as ad hoc fixes. The OPES framework contains no ad hoc fixes, and this document together with the other OPES documents should be sufficient to inform service creators of the IAB considerations. If a service does URI resolution or silently affects document reference validity, its authors are requested to review the service's impact on Internet application addressing architecture and to work within the IETF on potential extension requirements, which would be outside the current OPES framework.
sections.plainLanguage: Three smaller worries: a way to ask for the unmodified version, clarity that the services act on the result of resolving a name rather than on the resolving itself, and a rule that anything needing an architectural change must go to the IETF rather than be patched up locally.

sections.title: Privacy and Encryption
sections.content:
The IAB's privacy consideration is that the overall OPES framework must provide for mechanisms for end users to determine the privacy policies of OPES intermediaries. Tracing allows end users to identify OPES intermediaries, and it is required that the identification provided can be used to locate information about those intermediaries, including their privacy policies. The term privacy policy is not defined in this context by either the IAB or the OPES working group, but the memo records the belief that once an OPES system is identified, it would be possible to locate relevant information about that system, including information relevant to a requester's perception of the privacy policy or of reference validity.

On encryption, the IAB asked that the working group explicitly decide and document whether the OPES architecture must be compatible with the use of end-to-end encryption by one or more ends of an OPES-involved session. If OPES were compatible with end-to-end encryption, that would effectively ensure that OPES boxes would be restricted to ones that are known, trusted, explicitly addressed at the IP layer, and authorized by the provision of decryption keys by at least one of the ends. The quoted requirement was not explicitly listed as one of the IAB considerations but still needs to be addressed, and the context of the quote implies that end-to-end encryption refers to encryption along all links of the end-to-end path, with the OPES intermediaries as encrypting and decrypting participants or hops.

Since OPES processors are regular hops on the application protocol path, the architecture allows for such encryption, provided the application protocol being adapted supports it. Hop-by-hop encryption would do little good for overall message path protection if callout services have to receive unencrypted content. To allow for complete link encryption coverage, the OPES callout protocol supports encryption of connections between an OPES processor and a callout server through optional, negotiated transport encryption mechanisms. For example, TLS encryption can be used among HTTP hops, some of which could be OPES processors, and between each OPES processor and a callout server.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the trace identifies the device, a user can then look up what that device says it does with the data. And where the application protocol supports encryption, the whole path can be encrypted, including the link to the server doing the work.

viz.caption: THE NINE CONSIDERATIONS AND THE OPES ANSWER TO EACH

cells: The architecture requires that processors be consented to by the consumer or the provider application
Processors must be addressable at the IP layer by the end user; addressing the first processor in a chain is enough
Traces let a content provider see who adapted its content and what was done
Traces let an end user see the intermediaries in the path
OPES entities must support a bypass feature
Adaptations are documented as acting on the result of URI resolution, not on the resolving itself
The identification in the trace can be used to find information about the impact on reference validity
Services that break these rules are asked to take the problem to the IETF instead of fixing it locally
The identification lets a user find the privacy policy of an intermediary
